materials.text:
First, read from the Node.Ready() channel and process the updates it contains. These steps may be performed in parallel, except as noted in step 2.

1. Write Entries, HardState and Snapshot to persistent storage in order, i.e. Entries first, then HardState and Snapshot if they are not empty. If persistent storage supports atomic writes then all of them can be written together. Note that when writing an Entry with Index i, any previously-persisted entries with Index >= i must be discarded.

2. Send all Messages to the nodes named in the To field. It is important that no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk, and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch (Messages may be sent while entries from the same batch are being persisted). To reduce the I/O latency, an optimization can be applied to make leader write to disk in parallel with its followers (as explained at section 10.2.1 in Raft thesis). If any Message has type MsgSnap, call Node.ReportSnapshot() after it has been sent (these messages may be large). Note: Marshalling messages is not thread-safe; it is important to make sure that no new entries are persisted while marshalling. The easiest way to achieve this is to serialise the messages directly inside the main raft loop.

3. Apply Snapshot (if any) and CommittedEntries to the state machine. If any committed Entry has Type EntryConfChange, call Node.ApplyConfChange() to apply it to the node. The configuration change may be cancelled at this point by setting the NodeID field to zero before calling ApplyConfChange (but ApplyConfChange must be called one way or the other, and the decision to cancel must be based solely on the state machine and not external information such as the observed health of the node).

4. Call Node.Advance() to signal readiness for the next batch of updates. This may be done at any time after step 1, although all updates must be processed in the order they were returned by Ready.

Second, all persisted log entries must be made available via an implementation of the Storage interface. The provided MemoryStorage type can be used for this (if repopulating its state upon a restart), or a custom disk-backed implementation can be supplied.

Third, after receiving a message from another node, pass it to Node.Step:

```go
	func recvRaftRPC(ctx context.Context, m raftpb.Message) {
		n.Step(ctx, m)
	}
```

Finally, call `Node.Tick()` at regular intervals (probably via a `time.Ticker`). Raft has two important timeouts: heartbeat and the election timeout. However, internally to the raft package time is represented by an abstract "tick".

The total state machine handling loop will look something like this:

```go
  for {
    select {
    case <-s.Ticker:
      n.Tick()
    case rd := <-s.Node.Ready():
      saveToStorage(rd.HardState, rd.Entries, rd.Snapshot)
      send(rd.Messages)
      if !raft.IsEmptySnap(rd.Snapshot) {
        processSnapshot(rd.Snapshot)
      }

func TestNodeAdvance(t *testing.T) {
	storage := newTestMemoryStorage(withPeers(1))
	c := &Config{
		ID:              1,
		ElectionTick:    10,
		HeartbeatTick:   1,
		Storage:         storage,
		MaxSizePerMsg:   noLimit,
		MaxInflightMsgs: 256,
	}
	ctx, cancel, n := newNodeTestHarness(context.Background(), t, c)
	defer cancel()

	n.Campaign(ctx)
	// Persist vote.
	rd := readyWithTimeout(n)
	storage.Append(rd.Entries)
	n.Advance()
	// Append empty entry.
	rd = readyWithTimeout(n)
	storage.Append(rd.Entries)
	n.Advance()

	n.Propose(ctx, []byte("foo"))
	rd = readyWithTimeout(n)
	storage.Append(rd.Entries)
	n.Advance()
	select {
	case <-n.Ready():
	case <-time.After(100 * time.Millisecond):
		t.Errorf("expect Ready after Advance, but there is no Ready available")
	}
}

formation.explanation: Leader admits proposals, assigns term/index and emits append requests. Followers match predecessors, protect committed prefixes and defer append support until persistence. Leader tracks qualified replies and selects the active majority or both joint majorities, committing only an advancing current-term entry. It propagates commit through appends and bounded heartbeats; Ready/application consumes the prefix separately. Retry/probe/snapshot paths recover lagging replicas. Configuration application can recalculate commit with different quorum eligibility, but unlike append-reply advancement it does not release queued precommit reads.

context.explanation: Campaigns require promotable membership and scan committed entries after applied for pending configurations. Real campaigns persist votes, aggregate eligible votes and elect an up-to-date leader; pre-vote preserves the term until support is obtained. Higher terms, same-term leader traffic to candidates and quorum loss remove authority; transfer requires caught-up target and times out. Reset clears per-election votes, remote match, read quorum contexts and transfer. Old-term messages cannot contribute ordinary support; committed log prefixes and old snapshot completion survive. Recovery rebuilds term/vote/configuration/log from caller storage.

connection.explanation: Election log freshness and persistent term/vote constrain who may form future decisions; current-term commit and active voter quorums constrain advancement by that leader. Configurations take effect via ApplyConfChange, not at append. Their applied-history bookkeeping is consumed by campaign admission and proposal serialization. Thus application acknowledgement is authority-relevant. Delayed storage messages carry term/context to avoid using obsolete support, while committed decisions and application work are term-independent. Safe reads wait for current-term commitment and quorum context; pending precommit messages differ from the resettable readOnly map.

selections.rationale: A conditional cursor discrepancy is already explained at the code level, while the decisive caller-ordering permission remains conflicting. No execution can resolve that contract question. Preserve it for explicit authority and pursue a more discriminating source lead.

feedback.answered: For the early-Advance Candidate, nextEnts in raft_test.go persists unstable entries, runs delayed messages and advances raftLog.applied but does not apply configuration entries. The campaign test therefore supports the cursor guard but not the legality of deferring an actual configuration callback; NodeAdvance test exercises ordinary entries only. This question remains a scoped contract pause, not explained safety or a defect. Separately, source inspection identifies an independent read-authority discriminator: switchToConfig returns after local removal without changing StateLeader when StepDownOnRemoval is false; stepLeader rejects new proposals when local progress is absent but ReadIndex has no matching eligibility guard. ProgressTracker.IsSingleton tests only the incoming voter count and absence of outgoing voters. Hence its fast path may run for a removed leader when the sole voter is a different node. The next question is whether an API-driven committed removal can leave that node serving a ReadState after the survivor commits a later write. No source read so far requires stopping a removed node, but API applicability and the complete history still need checking.
remaining: Map the emitted ReadState assertion and its authority context; investigate a two-node committed removal through actual RawNode APIs, with StepDownOnRemoval=false and the strict persistence/application-before-Advance order.
Retain the stronger control StepDownOnRemoval=true and normal active singleton read path when constructing a discriminator.
